Backers of the proposition said state bond money is needed to stabilize research funding after President Donald Trump repeatedly attempted (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2026/07/research-grants-california-2/) to cut existing and future federal science grants.
The measure’s critics say Prop. 38 is well-intentioned but poorly designed because it overlooks the many established public and nonprofit university and hospital research labs in California. They also say California should not subsidize subsets of scientific research and instead should support research more broadly.
Sponsored message
CalMatters obtained documents that included the five-year business plan of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The plan was part of the formal affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute, which the two parties signed in August 2024. Among other details, the agreement requires the institute to pay UCLA 7.5% of the net revenue of any drugs and technologies developed by the institute’s staff. The institute is one of the founding tenants at a UCLA-owned research park in West Los Angeles, where the institute is leasing 235,000 square feet of research space, the institute says.
Far fewer employees than plan called for
Between summer 2024 and summer 2025, the institute committed to hiring “approximately” 51 employees, including six executives, five “world-class” scientists who can lead research labs, and 40 other employees, such as data scientists, lab technicians, biologists and administrative personnel. Between 2025 and 2027, the institute would hire roughly 90 more workers, including 10 research lab leaders, according to the agreement.
But John Mazziotta, a senior UCLA official who also serves as a board member (https://www.calimmunology.org/board-of-directors) of the immunology institute, last month said the institute has hired just three employees: a chief operating officer, a general counsel, and a scientific advisor, and “they're well into the search” for a director. Mazziotta, the CEO of UCLA Health and vice chancellor for health sciences at UCLA, made his comments during the Sept. 16 UC Regents meeting.
The Yes on Prop. 38 campaign has repeatedly refused to comment on whether the bond was written specifically for the immunology institute. Claudia Briggs, a spokesperson for the campaign, told CalMatters in July that whichever nonprofit receives the $4.2 billion portion of the bond fund should be a sophisticated one that “is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”
At a September press conference, a Yes on Prop. 38 spokesperson appeared to confirm CalMatters’ findings that only one institute currently qualifies to be the one to receive half the bond money. “It is very likely that CIII, which is a research institute affiliated with UCLA, will qualify for half of the funds under the current criteria,” said Robin Swanson. CIII is the initialism for the immunology institute.
According to the five-year plan, the institute was supposed to spend $25 million on personnel between 2024-25 and 2025-26 and $45 million total on operating expenses in that time, including maintenance, utilities and rent. It was also supposed to spend an additional $167 million in that time on capital expenses, such as construction and demolition. However, Mazziotta told UC regents that the institute had so far spent a total of $20 million on “operating expenses, hires” and other expenses.
Sponsored message
The Yes on 38 campaign refused CalMatters’ request to interview Michelson for this story, as did Michelson himself in a separate email. A spokesperson for the institute, Becky Warren, sent a written statement that didn't answer CalMatters' questions about employing far fewer people than the five-year plan laid out. Instead, she highlighted the promise of the institute and a few of its milestones, including signing the affiliation agreement with UCLA and clearing a state environmental review of its forthcoming research facility.
The institute won’t get state bond money if it isn’t ready to begin work, “plain and simple,” wrote Swanson, the Yes on 38 spokesperson, in an email. She stressed that though the institute very likely qualifies, the ultimate decision (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/#:~:text=The%20bond%20measure%20language%20says%20that%20if%20no%20institute%20qualifies%2C%20the%20California%20Department%20of%20Public%20Health%20can%20adjust%20the%20criteria%20to%20select%20a%20winning%20institute.%C2%A0) to award half the bond funding is up to the California Department of Public Health.
Institute facility will be built by 2028
The UCLA research park that houses the institute isn’t slated to be fully built until at least late 2028, according to the agenda item (https://regents.universityofcalifornia.edu/regmeet/sept26/f3.pdf) of the September UC regents meeting. The research park is a former mall UCLA acquired in late 2023 that’s now undergoing major retrofitting.
But the 2024 affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute anticipated this. The agreement permitted the institute to use UCLA health research space on another campus property on an interim basis. Mazziotta told regents that research is underway there.
Mazziotta also told the regents the institute's construction costs are not fully funded — it still needs roughly $100 million. He said UCLA was in serious talks with a donor to provide about $50 million to the institute.
If Prop. 38 passes, the bond funding would be provided in increments (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=shall%20not%20apply.-,130375.,-Solely%20for%20the) based on how often the institute requests new money that senior state officials approve. If all the funds are depleted, Californians would repay the bond (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) at a rate of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years.
Sponsored message
Institute would be exempt from public records act
CalMatters submitted the public records request to UCLA, which must comply with the California Public Records Act. The institute, as a private nonprofit, does not have to comply. And while Prop. 38 would channel billions of dollars in taxpayer money to the institute, the proposition’s language specifically exempts the nonprofit that will receive the $4.2 billion from state public meetings laws, political reform laws and the public records act. The other half of the funds would go to a council that’ll pick projects led by researchers from a limited pool of universities and nonprofits. The council would generally (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=The%20Political%20Reform%20Act%20of%201974%20(Title%209%20(commencing%20with%20Section%2081000)%20of%20the%20Government%20Code)%20shall%20apply%20to%20the%20council%2C%20except%20as%20provided%20in%20this%20section.) be governed by the state’s political reform act, which prohibits financial self-dealing.
Briggs defended the institute’s exemption in Prop. 38, writing that applying state transparency laws to existing private organizations would “not fit well with how private entities are organized and operate.” Instead, she noted the selected nonprofit institute would be required to publish annual reports on its research progress and financial plans plus commit to annual state audits, among other disclosures written into the ballot measure.
Still unclear to the UC regents is the relationship between UCLA and the institute on matters of public disclosure. Four senior UCLA officials sit on the institute’s board. So is a document held by those UCLA officials public because it’s related to UCLA affairs or private because it’s related to the institute’s affairs? UC’s general counsel couldn’t explain where that dividing line is after a regent member asked him. The regent member, Michael Cohen, said he wants more clarity when the regents meet again in November.
Gov. Gavin Newsom and the California Democratic Party endorsed (https://yeson38.com/newsroom/press-releases/) Prop. 38, as have dozens of patient and research advocacy groups, plus the state GOP. The union of graduate students and post-doctoral researchers, whose pay often relies on science research funding, has also endorsed the proposition. The union doesn’t represent faculty.
Money raised in support of Prop. 38 now exceeds $66 million, including at least $61.2 million in contributions from Michelson and his policy institute. Roughly $14 million of that includes loans from Michelson. The no camp has raised about $8,800

Now I have a very comprehensive picture. Key additional facts:

1. **League of Women Voters of California OPPOSES** Prop 38 — their reasoning: borrowing is a poor way to pay for research, locks billions into one field, and "California's stem-cell bond experience shows that royalties may do little to offset the debt."

2. **There's a competing/alternative legislative bond**: SB 895 (Wiener), signed by Newsom, puts a $7.5 billion California Science and Health Research Bond on the **March 2028 ballot**. It would create a state foundation awarding grants/loans through peer review across disciplines, with transparency protections. Opponents of Prop 38 argue voters should choose this instead — Panush: "There's only so much money you can invest in these kinds of things, and we don't believe that it's possible to do both."

3. Opposition includes: League of Women Voters, Common Cause California, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Orange County Register Editorial Board, Peace and Freedom Party, three retired LAO analysts (Marianne O'Malley, Dan Carson, and one more), Ruth Coleman (former State Parks director), Robert Kaplan (Stanford, former NIH associate director), David Panush (former Senate health policy advisor).

4. Support includes: Gov. Newsom, CA Democratic Party, CA GOP (interesting — both parties), Michael J. Fox Foundation, Alzheimer's Association/LA, ALS Association, American Nurses Association/CA, National MS Society, Prostate Cancer Foundation, Kidney Cancer Association, Melanoma Research Alliance, UAW grad students/postdocs union, San Diego County Democrats.

5. Editorial boards against: SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee/Modesto Bee/Merced Sun-Star/Fresno Bee/San Luis Obispo Tribune (McClatchy CA), Mercury News/East Bay Times, Press Democrat, Orange County Register, LAist republishing CalMatters critical reporting.

8. The institute (CIII): only 3 employees as of Sept 2026, facility not complete until late 2028, construction not fully funded (~$100 million short), exempt from public records act/open meeting laws/political reform act, UCLA officials on its board with unclear public/private document status.

- What did Prop 71/CIRM actually produce? The LWV mentioned "California's stem-cell bond experience shows that royalties may do little to offset the debt." Let me verify CIRM's royalty record — from what I know, CIRM funded ~$3 billion in bonds (2004) + $5.5 billion more (2020), and generated relatively modest royalty revenues (~$300-400 million or so). This is a relevant precedent for the "pays for itself" claim.
- Polling on Prop 38 to see where it stands (SF Chronicle editorial said "it's ahead in the polls").
- Maybe check the Yes on 38 campaign's responses to the criticisms, to be fair — e.g., the CBS piece with Robin Swanson, and their claims about accountability, the 20% discount, and federal cuts.
- Also check the Howard Jarvis/Orange County Register and any LA Times editorial. Did the LA Times weigh in? Let me search.

Let me also verify the "constitutional challenge" story and look at the actual text exemption language if possible. But given the extensive research already, the main remaining items are: CIRM precedent, LA Times position, polling, and the Yes campaign's best arguments.

Authorizes $8.4 billion in state bonds for immunology/immunotherapy research — half as competitive grants, but **half ($4.2 billion) guaranteed to a single unnamed UC-affiliated institute**, costing the General Fund $500–600 million per year for ~20 years.

California's own precedent is sobering: the $3 billion stem cell bond (Prop 71) promised billions in royalties and delivered a first royalty check of $190,346 — a negligible return.

Newsom just signed SB 895, placing a $7.5 billion science research bond on the **March 2028 ballot** — competitively awarded through peer review across disciplines, with full transparency protections. Even the No campaign's leaders say the state realistically can't fund both.

**5. Broad expert consensus against it.** Every editorial board I could find opposes it (SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee, Mercury News/East Bay Times, Fresno Bee, Press Democrat, Orange County Register), along with an unusual left-right coalition: League of Women Voters, Common Cause, and Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.

## What I weighed on the other side
Immunotherapy research is genuinely promising, federal science funding cuts are real, the cause has sincere backing (Michael J. Fox Foundation, Alzheimer's Association, both political parties, Gov. Newsom), and the grant half of the money is competitively distributed. But you can support medical research without handing $4.2 billion in debt-financed taxpayer money to an untested, three-employee institute created by the ballot measure's own billionaire financier — especially with a cleaner, competitive $7.5 billion alternative already slated for 2028.

**Vote No.**

Authorizes $8.4 billion in state bonds for immunology/immunotherapy research — half as competitive grants, but **half ($4.2 billion) guaranteed to a single unnamed UC-affiliated institute**, costing the General Fund $500–600 million per year for ~20 years.

## Why I land on No

**1. It's structured to funnel $4.2 billion to the measure's own sponsor.** The criteria for the "unnamed" institute (200,000+ sq ft space, affiliation with a UC health system serving 3.5M+ outpatients, a $50M "microbiome research program" donation, etc.) match exactly one entity in California: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy (CIII), co-founded by billionaire Gary Michelson — who wrote Prop 38 and has supplied virtually all of the ~$76–81 million Yes campaign (the No campaign has raised under $10,000). The Yes campaign's own spokesperson conceded CIII "very likely" qualifies.

**2. The institute isn't ready and would be exempt from transparency laws.** As of September 2026, CIII had just **3 employees** (vs. ~51 planned), no completed facility until late 2028, and ~$100 million unfunded construction costs. Despite receiving billions in public money, the measure explicitly exempts it from the Public Records Act, open-meeting laws, and the Political Reform Act. Three retired nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office analysts broke their tradition of silence to warn it "hijacks the initiative process to steer public funds to a billionaire's philanthropic project, and then hides its tracks."

**3. The "pays for itself" claim is speculative.** The LAO says revenue from discoveries is "uncertain" and could take decades to offset costs. California's own precedent is sobering: the $3 billion stem cell bond (Prop 71) promised billions in royalties and delivered a first royalty check of $190,346 — a negligible return.

**4. There's a better alternative coming.** Gov. Newsom just signed SB 895, placing a $7.5 billion science research bond on the **March 2028 ballot** — competitively awarded through peer review across disciplines, with full transparency protections. Even the No campaign's leaders say the state realistically can't fund both.

**5. Broad expert consensus against it.** Every editorial board I could find opposes it (SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee, Mercury News/East Bay Times, Fresno Bee, Press Democrat, Orange County Register), along with an unusual left-right coalition: League of Women Voters, Common Cause, and Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.

## What I weighed on the other side
Immunotherapy research is genuinely promising, federal science funding cuts are real, the cause has sincere backing (Michael J. Fox Foundation, Alzheimer's Association, both political parties, Gov. Newsom), and the grant half of the money is competitively distributed. But you can support medical research without handing $4.2 billion in debt-financed taxpayer money to an untested, three-employee institute created by the ballot measure's own billionaire financier — especially with a cleaner, competitive $7.5 billion alternative already slated for 2028.

**Vote No.**

PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants. Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue. Supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\CA Opponents: Robert M Kaplan Ph.D.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES on 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s. Strong accountability including independent audits. Mandates 20% Rx discount. Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers. YES on 38 could save your life and someone you love. Alzheimer’s Association, The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research urge YES on 38!
www.YESon38.com
CON
California should continue supporting biomedical research, but Proposition 38 is the wrong approach. It would commit taxpayers to decades of new bond debt while limiting California’s flexibility to address changing health priorities. Research funding should be guided through the normal budget process—not by ballot initiatives.

PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Medical Research and Development (R&D) Is a Multi- Stage Process. The first stage of this process is basic research, which focuses on discovering new knowledge about how the human body works. The next stage is applied and clinical research, which aims to develop and test treatments for specific diseases. Universities do most of the basic research, while companies do most of the applied and clinical research. The third R&D stage is to have regulators review new treatments to make sure they are safe and effective. If a new treatment is approved, then it may be used on patients. Most R&D projects do not make it through all of these stages.
Medical R&D Is Funded in Various Ways. Funding for medical R&D in the United States totaled about $300 billion in 2023. Companies and government agencies (such as the National Institutes of Health) are the major funding sources for R&D nationally and in California. Beyond these funding sources, California voters have approved two ballot measures- Proposition 71 (2004) and Proposition 14 (2020)- giving the state authority to issue general obligation bonds to fund specified medical research. Combined, the two measures allowed the state to issue $8.5 billion in bonds for stem cell research. Bonds are a way for the state to borrow money, then repay it with interest over time. A general obligation bond is typically repaid from the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) For more information about bonds, see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.
PROPOSAL
New Bond for Specified Medical Research. Proposition 38 allows the state to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond for research in immunology and immunotherapy. Immunology is the study of the body’s immune system and how it protects the body from abnormal cells and other causes of disease. Immunotherapy develops treatments that help the immune system fight diseases more effectively. The measure requires that at least $4.2 billion of the bond funds be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. No more than 2 percent of total bond funds may be used for state administrative costs. Payments on the bond would come from the state General Fund.
Supports a Research Institute. About half of the bond funds would go to a research institute specializing in immunology and immunotherapy. The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) would select the institute. The selected institute must meet several criteria, including criteria related to its size, funding, and collaboration with a University of California (UC) campus. The institute would use the bond funds for research. Each year, the institute must issue a public report on its activities and have an independent financial audit.
Supports Research Grants. A council would give out the other half of bond funds as competitive research grants focused on immunology and immunotherapy. The council would consist of representatives from 7 UC campuses and 10 to 15 other universities and nonprofit research institutions in California. The council would set research priorities and select grant recipients from among its member organizations. Similar to the institute, the council would have public reporting and audit requirements.
Requires 10 Percent of Revenue From Discoveries First Be Used to Repay the State. Proposition 38 requires that the institute, in consultation with CDPH, try to generate the most revenue possible from the funded research. (Research, for example, could lead to the development of a new medical treatment.) Ten percent of any revenue generated must be given to the state. This revenue must first go into the state General Fund until it repays the cost of the research bond (the amount borrowed plus the interest). Any additional revenue would be used for future immunology and immunotherapy research.
Has Two Other Notable Provisions.
Requires Purchases From California Suppliers. Grant recipients must buy at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers when reasonably possible.
Requires California Patient Discount. Any treatment developed through funded research and sold in California must generally be offered at a 20 percent discount.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost of $500 Million to $600 Million Annually for About 20 Years to Repay the Bond. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years . The annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 10 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up-front with money it already has.
Potential State Revenue From Research Discoveries. The state could receive revenue from research funded by Proposition 38. The amount of revenue is uncertain but could be significant. It would depend on how many research projects lead to marketable treatments and how much money any given treatment generates. The timing of these revenues and how long it would take to offset the state’s bond cost is also uncertain, but could take decades.
Potential Indirect Fiscal Effects. Proposition 38 likely would have some indirect fiscal effects, particularly on costs for state health programs (such as Medi-Cal, which pays for health care for low-income Californians). For example, if the funded research leads to new medical treatments, the average cost of patient care could either increase or decrease. As a result, the overall effect on program costs is uncertain.

ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 38
PATIENT ADVOCATES, DOCTORS, NURSES AND MEDICAL RESEARCHERS URGE YES ON PROP. 38
Leading patient advocates including the Alzheimer’s Association, Michael J. Fox Foundation, American Nurses Association\ California, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society and Prostate Cancer Foundation all urge YES on PROP. 38 because it could save your life and the life of someone you love.
“I was just weeks away from losing my life when a breakthrough immunotherapy gave me a second chance. Vote YES on PROP. 38 because every family facing a devastating diagnosis deserves this same hope.”
-Laurie Adami, Cancer Survivor and Patient Advocate, Los Angeles
YES ON PROP. 38-TO CURE AND PREVENT DISEASES THROUGH LIFE-SAVING IMMUNOLOGY RESEARCH
PROP. 38 accelerates development of breakthrough treatments and cures for the diseases that impact nearly every family. At least half of all funds are specifically dedicated to cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s research.
“Immunology harnesses the body’s immune system to detect and stop diseases. Today, breakthrough immunotherapies are already curing cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Promising research is underway to prevent diseases including Parkinson’s, heart disease, diabetes and more.”
-Mark Davis, Ph.D., Member of the National Academy of Sciences and the National Academy of Medicine
“One in nine people over 65 are living with Alzheimer’s, but there are currently no effective cures. YES on PROP. 38 provides real promise to find treatments and cures for the millions of patients and their families living with Alzheimer’s and dementia.”
-Susan Disney Lord, Board Chair of Alzheimer’s Los Angeles
HELPS OFFSET FEDERAL FUNDING CUTS TO MEDICAL RESEARCH
Massive federal funding cuts and uncertainty are disrupting vitally needed medical research at nonprofit research institutes and universities, delaying progress toward life-saving cures.
PROP. 38 creates a stable source of funding for breakthrough immunology research. All funds are dedicated exclusively to California-based nonprofit universities and research institutes- helping California lead the nation in medical innovation, fostering collaboration among top scientists and universities, and creating tens of thousands of good-paying jobs.
“Immunotherapy is transforming the future of cancer care. PROP. 38 will help accelerate life-saving cures while strengthening California’s role as a global leader in medical innovation.”
-Gina Carithers, President and CEO, Prostate Cancer Foundation
LOWERS HEALTHCARE COSTS FOR CALIFORNIANS
Any cure or immunotherapy developed through PROP. 38 must be provided to California patients at a 20% DISCOUNT. Preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will also reduce long-term healthcare expenses and save the state and families tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.
STRONG ACCOUNTABILITY & TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
PROP. 38 is designed to pay for itself WITH NO NET COST TO THE STATE OR TAXPAYERS. Ten percent of revenue from the licensing of successful immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset the costs of the bond, including interest.

2% Cap on State Administrative Expenses

YES ON PROP. 38: SUPPORTED BY DOCTORS, NURSES AND PATIENT ADVOCATES
• ALS Association • Alzheimer’s Association • American Nurses Association\California • Blood Cancer United • California Colorectal Cancer Coalition • Liver Coalition • Michael J. Fox Foundation • National Multiple Sclerosis Society • Parkinson Association of Northern California ... and many more.

Susan Disney Lord , Board Chair

Eugene P. Brandon , Ph.D., Board of Trustees

REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 38
California should continue supporting biomedical research. Everyone hopes for new treatments for heart disease, cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and other serious illnesses. I do too. But Proposition 38 is the wrong way to achieve that goal.
The claim that Proposition 38 will pay for itself is speculative. Audits, public disclosure, and limits on administrative costs promote accountability, but they cannot guarantee that research investments will generate enough economic returns to offset billions of dollars in bond repayments.
California faces a continuing structural budget deficit.
Proposition 38 would require approximately $8.4 billion in bond repayments. According to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, taxpayers would be committed to roughly $500 million in annual debt payments for the next 25 years. That long-term obligation would further reduce the state’s fiscal flexibility to respond to changing priorities.
Meanwhile, recent actions by the Trump administration have placed funding for essential California public health programs at risk, including disease surveillance, emergency preparedness, HIV prevention, vaccination infrastructure, laboratory capacity, and community prevention. These challenges extend well beyond biomedical research.
If California chooses to replace declining federal support, elected officials should be able to consider all health priorities together. Proposition 38 instead earmarks billions of borrowed dollars for one scientific field, regardless of future needs or discoveries. Research priorities should be guided through the normal budget process-not by ballot measures that lock taxpayers into decades of debt. Vote No on Proposition 38.
Robert M Kaplan , Ph.D.
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 38
California recognizes that continued investment in science is essential. But this proposition is not the best way to achieve that goal.
The measure would authorize approximately $8.4 billion in state borrowing to support immunology and immunotherapy research through a new University of California institute. Although the objective is appealing, the financing and policy framework are flawed.
First, the proposition continues the use of ballot initiatives to direct research funding toward selected topics. California has already created separate funding programs for stem cell research and precision medicine. This measure would add another highly focused program. Research priorities should be established through scientific review and public health planning-not by election campaigns. Cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and heart disease deserve attention, but so do mental illness, kidney disease, eye diseases, and many other conditions. Ballot-box science inevitably favors the most visible topics rather than the greatest scientific opportunities or public health needs.
Second, borrowing is an inappropriate way to finance scientific research. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the bonds authorized by this measure would obligate taxpayers to $500 million in annual debt payments for about 25 years. Bonds are commonly used for highways, schools, and other long-lived infrastructure with predictable benefits. Scientific research is different. Discoveries often require decades before they improve patient care, and many promising lines of investigation never produce marketable treatments.
Third, the proposition assumes that successful discoveries will generate revenues to offset state costs. In reality, universities rarely commercialize new therapies on their own. Publicly funded research lays the scientific foundation, but private companies typically invest the far greater resources required for product development, clinical testing, manufacturing, and regulatory approval. The public benefits are real, but they generally do not flow back to the state treasury.
Finally, the proposition requires certain therapies developed with state support to be sold in California at discounted prices. While this may sound attractive, it could incentivize companies to prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices are not controlled.
California should continue to support biomedical research. But research funding should be strategic, flexible, and fiscally responsible. Decisions about scientific priorities should be based on expert evaluation of emerging scientific opportunities and public health needs, not on a series of expensive ballot measures financed through long-term debt.
California has better options. For example, Senator Scott Wiener has proposed creating a state-funded research agency modeled on the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation. Rather than directing resources to specific areas of science, such an institution could establish priorities through expert scientific review and adapt its investments as new opportunities emerge. Although the legislation has not advanced, it received support from the University of California, the United Auto Workers, and the Union of American Physicians and Dentists. Similar legislation is likely to be considered in the future.
A “No” vote does not reject science. It rejects an inefficient financing mechanism and a fragmented approach to setting research priorities. California can and should support medical research through more coordinated, sustainable policies.
Robert M Kaplan , Ph.D.
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 38
YES ON PROP. 38 IS VITALLY NEEDED FOR LIFE-SAVING IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
Today, breakthrough immunotherapies are already curing cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Promising research is underway to cure and prevent diseases including Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s, ALS and more.
MASSIVE FEDERAL FUNDING CUTS ARE THREATENING PROGRESS TOWARD LIFE-SAVING CURES
YES on 38 will ensure California universities and nonprofit research institutions can continue vitally needed immunology research to cure and prevent the most debilitating diseases.
“Immunology saved my life-I now live cancer-free, and it could save millions of other lives too.”
-Andrew Dale, Immunotherapy Patient and Cancer Survivor
YES ON 38 IS DESIGNED TO PAY FOR ITSELF-WITH NO COST TO TAXPAYERS
Ten percent (10%) of revenue from licensing immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset bond costs. These requirements are locked into this measure.
YES ON 38 MANDATES STRONG ACCOUNTABILITY & TRANSPARENCY
2% Cap on State Administrative Expenses
Public Disclosure of Spending
Independent Financial Audits
YES ON 38 LOWERS HEALTHCARE COSTS
Immunotherapies developed through Prop. 38 must be provided to California patients at 20% discount. Preventing and curing diseases will also save families and the state billions of dollars in long-term healthcare expenses.
DOCTORS, NURSES AND PATIENT ADVOCATES URGE YES ON 38
• Alzheimer’s Association • American Nurses Association\ California • ALS Association • Kidney Cancer Association • Melanoma Research Alliance • National Multiple Sclerosis Society • The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research ... and many more.
Support Life-Saving Cures. Please Vote YES on 38.
www.YESon38.com
Andrew Dale , Cancer Survivor
Santa Monica
Anne M. Holloway , Board Member
The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research
Chris Tarver , R.N., President
American Nurses Association\California

This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. With just three workers, is it ready
CalMatters (https://laist.com/people/calmatters)
Mikhail Zinshteyn | CalMatters
Published October 20, 2026 at 3:00 PM PDT
Courtyard view of the UCLA Research Park under construction in the former Westside Pavilion shopping center in West Los Angeles on Aug. 19, 2024
( Brian van der Brug,
/
Los Angeles Times via Getty Images
)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today (https://support.laist.com/quick-donate?ms=prenote&utm_source=laist&utm_medium=onsite_prenote&utm_campaign=prenote&utm_content=control_v1).
The science research institute that would likely receive $4.2 billion in public taxpayer money if voters approve Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) this November had only three employees as of last month — far fewer than the 51 staffers it planned to have hired by last year.
Public statements and public records CalMatters (https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28824106-responsive-documents-26-7631-redacted-copy/?q=email&mode=document#document/p1) obtained raise questions about how well prepared the institute is to shepherd so much money if the bond measure passes.
Prop. 38 would allocate up to $8.4 billion in bonds for scientific research on diseases and cures concerning the immune system, with an emphasis on finding treatments for Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The ballot language stipulates that a single, unnamed research institute would receive half the bond’s money to conduct research and partner with other researchers if it meets highly specific criteria. Bonds are a type of debt that must be repaid.
Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s principal funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign.
More news
The Supreme Court rejects a DOJ push to separate California ballots (https://laist.com/news/politics/the-supreme-court-rejects-a-doj-push-to-separate-california-ballots)
The U.S. Supreme Court has denied a last-minute request from the Department of Justice to wade into its unprecedented feud with California over the state's voter rolls.
What we know so far about LA and OC voter turnout in the 2026 midterm election (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-midterm-voter-turnout-los-angeles-orange-county)
A look at how many showed up to vote in the Nov. 3 midterm election, either in person or by mail, and how it compares to previous elections.
Beware the ‘red mirage’ if California Republicans have an election night lead (https://laist.com/news/politics/red-mirage-california-republicans-election-night-lead)
Don’t be fooled by early election returns. It can take California weeks to tally votes, leading to ‘red mirages’ and ‘blue shifts.’
Backers of the proposition said state bond money is needed to stabilize research funding after President Donald Trump repeatedly attempted (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2026/07/research-grants-california-2/) to cut existing and future federal science grants.
The measure’s critics say Prop. 38 is well-intentioned but poorly designed because it overlooks the many established public and nonprofit university and hospital research labs in California. They also say California should not subsidize subsets of scientific research and instead should support research more broadly.
Sponsored message
CalMatters obtained documents that included the five-year business plan of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The plan was part of the formal affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute, which the two parties signed in August 2024. Among other details, the agreement requires the institute to pay UCLA 7.5% of the net revenue of any drugs and technologies developed by the institute’s staff. The institute is one of the founding tenants at a UCLA-owned research park in West Los Angeles, where the institute is leasing 235,000 square feet of research space, the institute says.
Far fewer employees than plan called for
Between summer 2024 and summer 2025, the institute committed to hiring “approximately” 51 employees, including six executives, five “world-class” scientists who can lead research labs, and 40 other employees, such as data scientists, lab technicians, biologists and administrative personnel. Between 2025 and 2027, the institute would hire roughly 90 more workers, including 10 research lab leaders, according to the agreement.
But John Mazziotta, a senior UCLA official who also serves as a board member (https://www.calimmunology.org/board-of-directors) of the immunology institute, last month said the institute has hired just three employees: a chief operating officer, a general counsel, and a scientific advisor, and “they're well into the search” for a director. Mazziotta, the CEO of UCLA Health and vice chancellor for health sciences at UCLA, made his comments during the Sept. 16 UC Regents meeting.
The Yes on Prop. 38 campaign has repeatedly refused to comment on whether the bond was written specifically for the immunology institute. Claudia Briggs, a spokesperson for the campaign, told CalMatters in July that whichever nonprofit receives the $4.2 billion portion of the bond fund should be a sophisticated one that “is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”
At a September press conference, a Yes on Prop. 38 spokesperson appeared to confirm CalMatters’ findings that only one institute currently qualifies to be the one to receive half the bond money. “It is very likely that CIII, which is a research institute affiliated with UCLA, will qualify for half of the funds under the current criteria,” said Robin Swanson. CIII is the initialism for the immunology institute.
According to the five-year plan, the institute was supposed to spend $25 million on personnel between 2024-25 and 2025-26 and $45 million total on operating expenses in that time, including maintenance, utilities and rent. It was also supposed to spend an additional $167 million in that time on capital expenses, such as construction and demolition. However, Mazziotta told UC regents that the institute had so far spent a total of $20 million on “operating expenses, hires” and other expenses.
Sponsored message
The Yes on 38 campaign refused CalMatters’ request to interview Michelson for this story, as did Michelson himself in a separate email. A spokesperson for the institute, Becky Warren, sent a written statement that didn't answer CalMatters' questions about employing far fewer people than the five-year plan laid out. Instead, she highlighted the promise of the institute and a few of its milestones, including signing the affiliation agreement with UCLA and clearing a state environmental review of its forthcoming research facility.
The institute won’t get state bond money if it isn’t ready to begin work, “plain and simple,” wrote Swanson, the Yes on 38 spokesperson, in an email. She stressed that though the institute very likely qualifies, the ultimate decision (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/#:~:text=The%20bond%20measure%20language%20says%20that%20if%20no%20institute%20qualifies%2C%20the%20California%20Department%20of%20Public%20Health%20can%20adjust%20the%20criteria%20to%20select%20a%20winning%20institute.%C2%A0) to award half the bond funding is up to the California Department of Public Health.
Institute facility will be built by 2028
The UCLA research park that houses the institute isn’t slated to be fully built until at least late 2028, according to the agenda item (https://regents.universityofcalifornia.edu/regmeet/sept26/f3.pdf) of the September UC regents meeting. The research park is a former mall UCLA acquired in late 2023 that’s now undergoing major retrofitting.
But the 2024 affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute anticipated this. The agreement permitted the institute to use UCLA health research space on another campus property on an interim basis. Mazziotta told regents that research is underway there.
Mazziotta also told the regents the institute's construction costs are not fully funded — it still needs roughly $100 million. He said UCLA was in serious talks with a donor to provide about $50 million to the institute.
If Prop. 38 passes, the bond funding would be provided in increments (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=shall%20not%20apply.-,130375.,-Solely%20for%20the) based on how often the institute requests new money that senior state officials approve. If all the funds are depleted, Californians would repay the bond (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) at a rate of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years.
Sponsored message
Institute would be exempt from public records act
CalMatters submitted the public records request to UCLA, which must comply with the California Public Records Act. The institute, as a private nonprofit, does not have to comply. And while Prop. 38 would channel billions of dollars in taxpayer money to the institute, the proposition’s language specifically exempts the nonprofit that will receive the $4.2 billion from state public meetings laws, political reform laws and the public records act. The other half of the funds would go to a council that’ll pick projects led by researchers from a limited pool of universities and nonprofits. ### Proposition 38
#### BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
Medical research can save lives, but Prop 38 is the wrong way to fund it.
It would authorize $8.4 billion in borrowing for immunology and immunotherapy research and require the state to make $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for about 20 years.
Those payments would come from the General Fund, which also pays for schools, health care, and other public services.
- **Borrowing is a poor way to pay for ongoing scientific research.** Bonds are best suited to long-lived investments such as buildings and infrastructure.
With interest, the Legislative Analyst estimates Prop 38 would cost about 10 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the research up front.
- **Prop 38 would lock billions of dollars into one field of research for years to come.** About half of the money would go to a single UC-affiliated research institute and the other half to a grant program, with at least $4.2 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research.

I've completed extensive research on Proposition 38 — the official voter guide and Legislative Analyst's analysis, investigative reporting from CalMatters, editorial positions from every major California newspaper, positions from good-government groups, the campaign finance records, the track record of California's previous medical research bonds, and the details of the alternative research bond already headed to the 2028 ballot.

# My answer: **NO**

## What Prop 38 does
Authorizes $8.4 billion in state bonds for immunology/immunotherapy research — half as competitive grants, but **half ($4.2 billion) guaranteed to a single unnamed UC-affiliated institute**, costing the General Fund $500–600 million per year for ~20 years.

## Why I land on No

**1. It's structured to funnel $4.2 billion to the measure's own sponsor.** The criteria for the "unnamed" institute (200,000+ sq ft space, affiliation with a UC health system serving 3.5M+ outpatients, a $50M "microbiome research program" donation, etc.) match exactly one entity in California: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy (CIII), co-founded by billionaire Gary Michelson — who wrote Prop 38 and has supplied virtually all of the ~$76–81 million Yes campaign (the No campaign has raised under $10,000). The Yes campaign's own spokesperson conceded CIII "very likely" qualifies.

**2. The institute isn't ready and would be exempt from transparency laws.** As of September 2026, CIII had just **3 employees** (vs. ~51 planned), no completed facility until late 2028, and ~$100 million unfunded construction costs. Despite receiving billions in public money, the measure explicitly exempts it from the Public Records Act, open-meeting laws, and the Political Reform Act. Three retired nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office analysts broke their tradition of silence to warn it "hijacks the initiative process to steer public funds to a billionaire's philanthropic project, and then hides its tracks."

**3. The "pays for itself" claim is speculative.** The LAO says revenue from discoveries is "uncertain" and could take decades to offset costs. California's own precedent is sobering: the $3 billion stem cell bond (Prop 71) promised billions in royalties and delivered a first royalty check of $190,346 — a negligible return.

**4. There's a better alternative coming.** Gov. Newsom just signed SB 895, placing a $7.5 billion science research bond on the **March 2028 ballot** — competitively awarded through peer review across disciplines, with full transparency protections. Even the No campaign's leaders say the state realistically can't fund both.

**5. Broad expert consensus against it.** Every editorial board I could find opposes it (SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee, Mercury News/East Bay Times, Fresno Bee, Press Democrat, Orange County Register), along with an unusual left-right coalition: League of Women Voters, Common Cause, and Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.

## What I weighed on the other side
Immunotherapy research is genuinely promising, federal science funding cuts are real, the cause has sincere backing (Michael J. Fox Foundation, Alzheimer's Association, both political parties, Gov. Newsom), and the grant half of the money is competitively distributed. But you can support medical research without handing $4.2 billion in debt-financed taxpayer money to an untested, three-employee institute created by the ballot measure's own billionaire financier — especially with a cleaner, competitive $7.5 billion alternative already slated for 2028.

**Vote No.**
